concepts: Angles of elevation and complementary angles (heights and distances)
questions.question: Two vertical poles are $150$ m apart and the height of one is three times that of the other. If from the middle point of the line joining their feet, an observer finds the angles of elevation of their tops to be complementary, then the height of the shorter pole (in meters) is :
solution: Let the shorter pole have height $h$, so the taller has height $3h$. The observer is at the midpoint, $75$ m from each foot.
Let $\theta$ and $\phi$ be the angles of elevation of the tops of the taller and the shorter pole, with $\theta+\phi=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Complementary elevations mean the two lines of sight are perpendicular, so their dot product is zero.
solution: Put the observer at the origin $O$, with the shorter pole on the right at $x=75$ and the taller on the left at $x=-75$.

The tops are $T_1(75,\,h)$ and $T_2(-75,\,3h)$. The elevations are complementary exactly when $OT_1\perp OT_2$ (the angles $\phi$ and $\theta$ together with the right angle between the lines of sight fill $180^\circ$).

useful_results: Complementary angles of elevation $\iff$ $\tan\theta\tan\phi=1\iff$ the lines of sight to the two tops are perpendicular.
If the observer is at distances $d_1,d_2$ from the feet of poles of heights $h_1,h_2$ and the elevations are complementary, then $h_1h_2=d_1d_2$. At the midpoint $d_1=d_2=d/2$, so $h_1h_2=(d/2)^2$.
Here $h\cdot3h=75^2$ gives $h=25\sqrt3$; the ratio $h_1:h_2$ can be anything, only the product is fixed.

concepts: Angle of elevation with uniform speed (heights and distances)
questions.question: The angle of elevation of a jet plane from a point A on the ground is $60^\circ$. After a flight of $20$ seconds at the speed of $432$ km/hour, the angle of elevation changes to $30^\circ$. If the jet plane is flying at a constant height, then its height is:
questions.key_idea: At constant height the horizontal shift is $h\cot30^\circ-h\cot60^\circ$.
solution: Let the plane move from $B'$ to $C'$ at constant height $h$; $B$ and $C$ are the points on the ground directly below.
The elevations from $A$ are $60^\circ$ at $B'$ and $30^\circ$ at $C'$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Exterior-angle theorem: the elevation halves from $60^\circ$ to $30^\circ$, so triangle $AB'C'$ is isosceles.
solution: $B'C'$ is horizontal and $AB'$ makes $60^\circ$ with the ground, so $\angle AB'C'=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$.
The speed gives $B'C'=2400$ m, so $AB'=2400$ m.
The height is $h=AB'\sin60^\circ=2400\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=1200\sqrt3$ m. Same answer.

useful_results: Plane (or object) at constant height $h$, elevations $\alpha>\beta$ from the same ground point: horizontal distance covered $=h(\cot\beta-\cot\alpha)$.
Unit conversion: $1$ km/h $=\dfrac{5}{18}$ m/s, so $432$ km/h $=120$ m/s.
If the elevation drops from $2\theta$ to $\theta$ (here $60^\circ\to30^\circ$), the distance flown equals the first line of sight: $B'C'=AB'$ (exterior angle $2\theta=\theta+\theta$).

concepts: Angle of depression and uniform speed (heights and distances)
questions.question: A man is observing, from the top of a tower, a boat speeding towards the tower from a certain point A, with uniform speed. At that point, angle of depression of the boat with the man's eye is $30^\circ$ (Ignore man's height). After sailing for $20$ seconds, towards the base of the tower (which is at the level of water), the boat has reached a point B, where the angle of depression is $45^\circ$. Then the time taken (in seconds) by the boat from B to reach the base of the tower is :
questions.key_idea: At uniform speed time is proportional to distance, so find $AB:BC$ from the two depression angles.
solution: Let $D$ be the man's eye, $C$ the base of the tower, $DC=h$; let $AB=x$ (sailed in $20$ s) and $BC=y$.
Angles of depression equal angles of elevation from the boat: $\angle DAC=30^\circ$, $\angle DBC=45^\circ$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Apply the sine rule in $\triangle ABD$, where the angle at $D$ is the difference $45^\circ-30^\circ$.
solution: In $\triangle ABD$: $\angle DAB=30^\circ$, $\angle DBC=45^\circ$ is the exterior angle at $B$, so $\angle ADB=45^\circ-30^\circ=15^\circ$.

useful_results: Uniform speed: time $\propto$ distance, so only the ratio of distances is needed (the height cancels).

With depressions $\alpha$ (first) and $\beta$ (second), $\beta>\alpha$, the time still needed after the second point is $t_2=t\cdot\dfrac{\cot\beta}{\cot\alpha-\cot\beta}$, where $t$ is the time between the two observations.
Here $t_2=20\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3-1}=10(\sqrt3+1)$; check: $\cot45^\circ=1$, $\cot30^\circ=\sqrt3$.
Angle of depression from above $=$ angle of elevation from below (alternate angles).

concepts: Angle of elevation from the corners of a triangle (heights and distances)
Circumcentre and circumradius of a triangle
questions.question: A pole stands vertically inside a triangular park $ABC$. Let the angle of elevation of the top of the pole from each corner of the park be $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. If the radius of the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ is $2$, then the height of the pole is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Equal elevations from $A,B,C$ put the foot of the pole at the circumcentre, so $h=R\tan\alpha$.
solution: Let $P$ be the top of the pole and $O$ its foot; the elevation of $P$ from each of $A,B,C$ is $\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
Since $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{h}{OA}=\dfrac{h}{OB}=\dfrac{h}{OC}$, we get $OA=OB=OC$, so $O$ is the circumcentre and $OA=OB=OC=R=2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Triangle $POA$ is a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle: the leg opposite $30^\circ$ is $R$ and the leg opposite $60^\circ$ is $h$.
solution: As before $O$ is the circumcentre, so $OA=R=2$ and $\angle POA=90^\circ$, $\angle PAO=60^\circ$, hence $\angle APO=30^\circ$.
In a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle the sides are in the ratio $1:\sqrt3:2$, with $OA$ (opposite $30^\circ$) the shortest side.
Check with the slant edge: $PA=2\,OA=4$, and $h=\sqrt{PA^2-OA^2}=\sqrt{16-4}=2\sqrt3$. Same answer.

useful_results: Equal angles of elevation from all vertices of a polygon $\Rightarrow$ the foot of the pole is equidistant from them, i.e. the circumcentre; then $h=R\tan\alpha$.
Equal angles of elevation from all the sides (perpendicular distances to the sides) $\Rightarrow$ the foot is the incentre and $h=r\tan\alpha$.
Here $h=2\tan60^\circ=2\sqrt3$; the circumradius can be found from $R=\dfrac{a}{2\sin A}$ when the triangle is given.

concepts: Angle subtended by a sphere and angle of elevation (heights and distances)
Trigonometric values of $75^\circ$ (compound angles)
questions.question: A spherical gas balloon of radius $16$ meter subtends an angle $60^\circ$ at the eye of the observer A while the angle of elevation of its center from the eye of A is $75^\circ$. Then the height (in meter) of the top most point of the balloon from the level of the observer's eye is :
questions.key_idea: The tangent lines make $30^\circ$ with $AO$, so $AO=\dfrac{r}{\sin30^\circ}$; then add the radius to the centre's height.
solution: Let $O$ be the centre of the balloon and $AD$ a tangent from the eye $A$ touching at $D$, with $OD=16$ and $OD\perp AD$.
The balloon subtends $60^\circ$ at $A$, so the line $AO$ bisects it: $\angle OAD=30^\circ$.
Let $B$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to the horizontal line through $A$. In $\triangle OAB$: $\sin75^\circ=\dfrac{OB}{AO}$, so $OB=32\sin75^\circ$.
The topmost point $E$ is the radius above the centre: $BE=BO+OE=8\sqrt2(\sqrt3+1)+16$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes 'BE = BO + OA = 8√2(√3+1) + 16', but OA = 32; the 16 added is the radius OE. Label corrected to BE = BO + OE (the numbers and the answer are unchanged).

alternate_solutions.idea: Locate the centre by coordinates: tangent point $D$ on the lower $45^\circ$ line, then move one radius perpendicular to it.
solution: Take the eye $A$ as origin. The lower tangent makes $75^\circ-30^\circ=45^\circ$ with the horizontal and touches at $D$ with $AD=\sqrt{32^2-16^2}=16\sqrt3$ (using $AO=32$).
$OD\perp AD$ and $OD=16$, so the centre is $O=D+16(-\sin45^\circ,\cos45^\circ)=(8\sqrt6-8\sqrt2,\;8\sqrt6+8\sqrt2)$.
The height of the centre is $8\sqrt6+8\sqrt2$ (check: $\dfrac{y_O}{x_O}=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}=2+\sqrt3=\tan75^\circ$).
Top point $=$ centre $+16$ $=8(\sqrt6+\sqrt2+2)$ m. Same answer, with no value of $\sin75^\circ$ needed.

useful_results: A sphere of radius $r$ seen from a point at distance $D$ from its centre subtends an angle $2\gamma$ with $\sin\gamma=\dfrac{r}{D}$ (the tangent cone).
The highest point of a sphere is its centre's height $+\,r$; the lowest is centre's height $-\,r$.
$\sin75^\circ=\cos15^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}$ and $\sin15^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}$ (from $\sin(45^\circ\pm30^\circ)$). Check: $32\sin75^\circ+16\approx46.91=8(\sqrt6+\sqrt2+2)$.

concepts: Angle between space diagonals of a cuboid (vectors and 3D geometry)
questions.question: A hall has a square floor of dimension $10$ m $\times$ $10$ m (see the figure) and vertical walls. If the angle $GPH$ between the diagonals $AG$ and $BH$ is $\cos^{-1}\dfrac{1}{5}$, then the height of the hall (in meters) is : (The hall is the cuboid $ABCD$-$EFGH$; the diagonals $AG$ and $BH$ meet at $P$.)
questions.key_idea: Put coordinates on the cuboid and use $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\vec{AG}\cdot\vec{BH}}{|\vec{AG}||\vec{BH}|}$.
solution: Take coordinates (with $y$ vertical) $A(0,0,0)$, $B(10,0,0)$, $G(10,h,10)$, $H(0,h,10)$, where $h$ is the height of the hall.
$\overrightarrow{BH}=-10\hat i+h\hat j+10\hat k$ and $\overrightarrow{AG}=10\hat i+h\hat j+10\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the cosine rule in the isosceles triangle $GPH$ whose base $GH$ is a roof edge of length $10$.
solution: The diagonals of a cuboid bisect each other at $P$, so $PG=PH=\dfrac12\sqrt{10^2+10^2+h^2}=\dfrac12\sqrt{200+h^2}$.
The roof edge $GH=10$ is opposite the angle $\angle GPH=\theta$.

useful_results: In a cuboid with edges $a,b,c$ the diagonals meet at the centre $P$; the angle $\psi$ they subtend opposite an edge of length $a$ satisfies $\cos\psi=\dfrac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{a^2+b^2+c^2}$.
Here $a=b=10$, $c=h$: $\cos\psi=\dfrac{h^2}{200+h^2}$. Cube check ($h=10$): $\cos\psi=\dfrac13$, the familiar angle between the diagonals of a cube.
The other angle between the same two diagonals is the supplement, $\pi-\psi$; check which one the question means (here it is $\angle GPH$, opposite the roof edge).

concepts: Angles of elevation of two poles (heights and distances)
Cotangent of a sum of angles
questions.question: Two poles, $AB$ of length $a$ metres and $CD$ of length $a+b$ ($b\neq a$) metres are erected at the same horizontal level with bases at $B$ and $D$. If $BD=x$ and $\tan\angle ACB=\dfrac12$, then :
solution: Let $\alpha=\angle ACB$ and $\beta=\angle BCD$, so $\angle ACD=\alpha+\beta$. The line $CA$ makes angle $90^\circ-(\alpha+\beta)$ with the horizontal through $A$, and the rise from $A$ to $C$ is $b$ over a run $x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $\tan\angle ACB$ directly as the angle between the lines $CA$ and $CB$ using cross and dot products.
solution: Set this equal to $\dfrac12$: $x^2+b(a+b)=2ax$, i.e. $x^2-2ax+b(a+b)=0$. Same answer, with no compound-angle formula.

useful_results: Angle between two lines of slopes $m_1,m_2$: $\tan\theta=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|$; equivalently $\tan\theta=\dfrac{|\vec u\times\vec v|}{\vec u\cdot\vec v}$ for the lines of sight to the two ends of a segment.
For poles of heights $a$ and $a+b$ a distance $x$ apart, the angle subtended at the top $C$ of the taller by the foot-to-top of the shorter satisfies $\tan\angle ACB=\dfrac{ax}{x^2+b(a+b)}$.
The subtended angle is largest when $x^2=b(a+b)$; so $\tan\angle ACB=\tfrac12$ is possible only if $a^2\ge b(a+b)$, which is the condition for real roots here.
Check: $a=2,b=1$ gives $x^2-4x+3=0$, $x=1$ or $3$; for $x=3$: $\dfrac{2\cdot3}{9+3}=\dfrac12$.

concepts: Equal angles subtended by two parts of a pole (heights and distances)
Angle bisector theorem
questions.question: A vertical pole fixed to the horizontal ground is divided in the ratio $3:7$ by a mark on it with lower part shorter than the upper part. If the two parts subtend equal angles at a point on the ground $18$ m away from the base of the pole, then the height of the pole (in meters) is :
questions.key_idea: Equal angles mean the line of sight to the mark bisects the angle at the observer, so the angle bisector theorem applies.
solution: Let $AC$ be the pole with $A$ at its base, $D$ the mark with $AD=3x$, $DC=7x$, and let $B$ be the observer with $AB=18$.
The parts $AD$ and $DC$ subtend equal angles $\alpha$ at $B$, so $BD$ bisects $\angle ABC$.
In the right triangle $ABC$ (right angle at $A$): $AC=\sqrt{BC^2-AB^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\tan2\alpha$ for the whole pole against $\tan\alpha$ for the lower part.
solution: Let the lower part be $3x$ and the whole pole $10x$; the lower part subtends $\alpha$ and the whole pole $2\alpha$ at $B$.

useful_results: A segment $PQ$ and a point $M$ on it subtend equal angles at $O$ exactly when $OM$ bisects $\angle POQ$; then $PM:MQ=OP:OQ$.

For a pole divided $m:n$ (lower : upper, $n>m$) with equal angles at a point $d$ from the base, the distance to the top is $d\,\dfrac nm$ and the height is $\dfrac{d}{m}\sqrt{n^2-m^2}$. Here $\dfrac{18}{3}\sqrt{49-9}=12\sqrt{10}$.
If $n\le m$ (upper part not longer than the lower) no such point exists.

concepts: Angles of elevation of two poles (heights and distances)
Values of $\tan\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ (half-angle formula)
questions.question: Let $AB$ and $PQ$ be two vertical poles, $160$ m apart from each other. Let $C$ be the middle point of $B$ and $Q$, which are feet of these two poles. Let $\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ and $\theta$ be the angles of elevation from $C$ to $P$ and $A$, respectively. If the height of pole $PQ$ is twice the height of pole $AB$, then $\tan^2\theta$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Since $BC=CQ$, the heights are in the ratio of the tangents of the elevations: $\tan\theta=\tfrac12\tan\tfrac\pi8$.
solution: Let $AB=x$ and $PQ=2x$. $C$ is the midpoint of $BQ$, so $BC=CQ=80$ m.

alternate_solutions.idea: Square the ratio first and use the half-angle identity $\tan^2\dfrac\pi8=\dfrac{1-\cos\frac\pi4}{1+\cos\frac\pi4}$, so $\tan\frac\pi8$ itself is never needed.

useful_results: At the same horizontal distance, heights are proportional to the tangents of the elevations: $\dfrac{h_1}{h_2}=\dfrac{\tan\alpha_1}{\tan\alpha_2}$.
$\tan\dfrac\pi8=\sqrt2-1$, $\tan\dfrac{\pi}{12}=2-\sqrt3$, $\tan\dfrac{3\pi}{8}=\sqrt2+1$, $\tan\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=2+\sqrt3$ (from $\tan\dfrac x2=\dfrac{1-\cos x}{\sin x}$).
The distance $160$ m is not needed: it cancels in the ratio. Check: $(\sqrt2-1)^2\approx0.1716=3-2\sqrt2$.

concepts: Angle subtended by a pole at the top of a tower (heights and distances)
questions.question: From the base of a pole of height $20$ meter, the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is $60^\circ$. The pole subtends an angle $30^\circ$ at the top of the tower. Then the height of the tower is :
questions.key_idea: The $30^\circ$ subtended at the top of the tower means the elevation of the tower top from the pole's top is $60^\circ-30^\circ=30^\circ$.
solution: Let the pole be $AB$ ($B$ its base, $AB=20$), the tower $CD$ (with $BC=d$), and $E$ the point on $CD$ level with $A$, with $DE=X$ the part of the tower above $A$.
The elevation of $D$ from $B$ is $60^\circ$, and the pole subtends $30^\circ$ at $D$, so the elevation of $D$ from $A$ is $60^\circ-30^\circ=30^\circ$ (exterior angle).
Height of the tower $=20+10=30$ m, option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Triangle $ABD$ has two equal angles of $30^\circ$, so it is isosceles with $AD=AB=20$.
solution: In $\triangle ABD$: $\angle ABD=90^\circ-60^\circ=30^\circ$ (between the vertical pole and the line of sight) and $\angle ADB=30^\circ$ (given).
Then $\angle BAD=180^\circ-30^\circ-30^\circ=120^\circ$, so $AD$ rises at $120^\circ-90^\circ=30^\circ$ above the horizontal through $A$.
The tower top is $AD\sin30^\circ=20\cdot\tfrac12=10$ m above $A$.

useful_results: The angle subtended at $D$ by a segment $AB$ equals the difference of the angles of elevation of $D$ from its ends: here $60^\circ-30^\circ$ (exterior-angle theorem).

For a pole $AB$ of length $p$, elevation $\theta$ of the top $D$ from the base $B$, and the pole subtending $\delta$ at $D$: $AD=\dfrac{p\cos\theta}{\sin\delta}$ and the tower height is $p+AD\sin(\theta-\delta)$.
Here $AD=\dfrac{20\cos60^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}=20$ and the height is $20+20\sin30^\circ=30$.

concepts: Angle subtended by part of a tower (heights and distances)
Values of $\tan75^\circ$ (compound angles)
questions.question: A tower $PQ$ stands on a horizontal ground with base $Q$ on the ground. The point $R$ divides the tower in two parts such that $QR=15$ m. If from a point $A$ on the ground the angle of elevation of $R$ is $60^\circ$ and the part $PR$ of the tower subtends an angle of $15^\circ$ at $A$, then the height of the tower is :
solution: Let $PR=x$. From $A$, the elevation of $R$ is $60^\circ$, so $\dfrac{15}{AQ}=\tan60^\circ$ ...(1).
The part $PR$ subtends $15^\circ$ at $A$, so the elevation of $P$ is $60^\circ+15^\circ=75^\circ$: $\dfrac{15+x}{AQ}=\tan75^\circ$ ...(2).

alternate_solutions.idea: Triangle $ARP$ has angles $15^\circ,150^\circ,15^\circ$, so it is isosceles with $RP=RA$.

useful_results: A segment of a vertical tower subtends at $A$ the difference of the elevations of its ends: $\angle PAR=\angle PAQ-\angle RAQ$.
$\tan75^\circ=\tan(45^\circ+30^\circ)=2+\sqrt3$ and $\tan15^\circ=2-\sqrt3$, so $\tan15^\circ\tan75^\circ=1$.
When a subtended angle equals another angle in the figure (here $\angle RAP=\angle APR=15^\circ$), look for an isosceles triangle before using tangents. Check: $15+10\sqrt3\approx32.32=5(2\sqrt3+3)$.

concepts: Angle of elevation after moving a distance (heights and distances)
Double-angle formula for $\tan2\alpha$ and a quadratic in $\tan\alpha$
questions.question: Let a vertical tower $AB$ of height $2h$ stand on a horizontal ground. Let from a point $P$ on the ground a man can see up to height $h$ of the tower with an angle of elevation $2\alpha$. When from $P$, he moves a distance $d$ in the direction of $\overrightarrow{AP}$, he can see the top $B$ of the tower with an angle of elevation $\alpha$. If $d=\sqrt7\,h$, then $\tan\alpha$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Eliminate $x=AP$ with $x=h\cot2\alpha$ and put $\tan\alpha=t$ to get a quadratic.
solution: Let $AP=x$ and let $C$ be the point at height $h$ on the tower. From $P$: $\tan2\alpha=\dfrac{h}{x}$.
After moving $d=\sqrt7h$ further from the tower (to $H$), the distance to the foot is $x+\sqrt7h$ and the elevation of $B$ is $\alpha$: $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{2h}{x+\sqrt7h}$.
Since $0<2\alpha<90^\circ$, $\tan\alpha<1$; the root $\sqrt7+2>1$ is rejected. So $\tan\alpha=\sqrt7-2$, option (C).
questions.correction_note: The PDF stops at 'Put tan α = t & simplify' and states tan α = √7 − 2. The algebra (quadratic t² − 2√7 t + 3 = 0) and the rejection of the second root √7 + 2 (> 1, impossible since 2α < 90°) were added. The answer is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the identity $\cot\alpha-\cot2\alpha=\csc2\alpha$ to turn the two sight lines into one equation in $u=x/h$.

useful_results: Identity: $\cot\alpha-\cot2\alpha=\csc2\alpha$ (and $\cot\alpha+\tan\alpha=2\csc2\alpha$). Check $\alpha=30^\circ$: $\sqrt3-\tfrac1{\sqrt3}=\tfrac2{\sqrt3}=\csc60^\circ$.
Moving a distance $d$ directly away from the tower changes the horizontal distance from $x$ to $x+d$, so $d=H(\cot\beta-\cot\alpha)$ for elevations $\alpha>\beta$ of a point at height $H$.

When the two elevations are $2\alpha$ and $\alpha$, convert everything to $t=\tan\alpha$ using $\tan2\alpha=\dfrac{2t}{1-t^2}$, then reject roots that make an angle impossible ($2\alpha<90^\circ\Rightarrow t<1$).

concepts: Angles of elevation in a vertical plane (heights and distances)
Area of a trapezium
questions.question: The angle of elevation of the top $P$ of a vertical tower $PQ$ of height $10$ from a point $A$ on the horizontal ground is $45^\circ$. Let $R$ be a point on $AQ$ and from a point $B$, vertically above $R$, the angle of elevation of $P$ is $60^\circ$. If $\angle BAQ=30^\circ$, $AB=d$ and the area of the trapezium $PQRB$ is $\alpha$, then the ordered pair $(d,\alpha)$ is :
questions.key_idea: Express $QR$ and $BR$ through $d$ (using $\angle BAQ=30^\circ$) and apply $\tan60^\circ$ to the right triangle formed by $P$, $B$ and the horizontal through $B$.
solution: In the right triangle $ARB$: $RA=d\cos30^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt3d}{2}$ and $BR=d\sin30^\circ=\dfrac d2$.
The elevation of $P$ from $B$ is $60^\circ$; the vertical rise from $B$ to $P$ is $PQ-BR=10-\dfrac d2$ over the horizontal run $QR$: $\tan60^\circ=\dfrac{10-\frac d2}{10-\frac{\sqrt3d}{2}}$.
Area of the trapezium ($PQ\parallel BR$, distance between them $QR$): $\alpha=\dfrac12(PQ+BR)\cdot QR=\dfrac12\left(10+\dfrac d2\right)\left(10-\dfrac{\sqrt3d}{2}\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: In triangle $ABP$ the angles at $A$ and $P$ are both $15^\circ$, so $BA=BP$; then $d$ follows from one line and the area from subtraction.
solution: $A,B,P,Q,R$ lie in one vertical plane. $AP$ makes $45^\circ$ and $AB$ makes $30^\circ$ with the ground, so $\angle BAP=15^\circ$.
$PB$ is inclined at $60^\circ$ below the horizontal at $P$ while $PA$ is inclined at $45^\circ$, so $\angle APB=60^\circ-45^\circ=15^\circ$.
So $\triangle ABP$ is isosceles with $BA=BP=d$ and base $AP=10\sqrt2$.

Area of the trapezium $=$ area of $\triangle APQ$ $-$ $\triangle ABR$ $-$ $\triangle ABP$. Here $[APQ]=50$, $[ABR]=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt3d}{2}\cdot\dfrac d2=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{8}d^2$, $[ABP]=\dfrac12d^2\sin150^\circ=\dfrac{d^2}{4}$.

useful_results: A line of sight at elevation $\theta$ from a point and another at $\phi$ from the same point (same vertical plane) enclose $|\theta-\phi|$; equal angles in a triangle give equal sides, which often replaces a tangent equation.
Area of a trapezium $=\dfrac12(\text{sum of the parallel sides})\times(\text{distance between them})$; two vertical segments are parallel and their distance is the horizontal gap.

A point at distance $d$ along a line inclined at $\theta$ has horizontal and vertical components $d\cos\theta$, $d\sin\theta$. Check: $d=7.32$, $BR=3.66$, $QR=3.66$, $PQ-BR=6.34$, ratio $6.34/3.66=\sqrt3$.

concepts: Angle of elevation in a triangular park (heights and distances)
Right triangles, Pythagoras and $\cot15^\circ$
questions.question: A horizontal park is in the shape of a triangle $OAB$ with $AB=16$. A vertical lamp post $OP$ is erected at the point $O$ such that $\angle PAO=\angle PBO=15^\circ$ and $\angle PCO=45^\circ$, where $C$ is the midpoint of $AB$, Then $(OP)^2$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Equal elevations from $A$ and $B$ make $OA=OB$, so $OC\perp AB$; then $OP=OC$ from $45^\circ$ and $OA=OP\cot15^\circ$.
solution: In $\triangle POA$: $\dfrac{OP}{OA}=\tan15^\circ$, so $OA=OP\cot15^\circ$. In $\triangle POB$ the same relation gives $OB=OA$, so $OC\perp AB$ ($C$ is the midpoint of the base of the isosceles triangle $OAB$).
In the right triangle $OCA$: $AC=8$, so $OC=\sqrt{OA^2-8^2}$, i.e. $OP=\sqrt{OA^2-8^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: By the three-perpendiculars theorem $PC\perp AB$, so $\triangle PCA$ is right-angled at $C$; use $PA=\dfrac{OP}{\sin15^\circ}$ and $PC=OP\sqrt2$.
solution: $OP\perp$ plane and $OC\perp AB$ (as $OA=OB$), so $PC\perp AB$ and $\triangle PCA$ is right-angled at $C$ with $AC=8$.

useful_results: If $P$ is above the point $O$ of a horizontal plane and $OC\perp AB$ in that plane, then $PC\perp AB$ (theorem of three perpendiculars); the triangle $PCA$ is right-angled at $C$.
Equal elevations of a pole's top from two points $\iff$ the foot of the pole is equidistant from them, so it lies on their perpendicular bisector.
$\cot15^\circ=2+\sqrt3$, $\cot^215^\circ=7+4\sqrt3$, $\sin^215^\circ=\dfrac{2-\sqrt3}{4}$. Check: $OP^2\approx4.95$, $OA=OP\cot15^\circ\approx8.30$, $\sqrt{OA^2-64}\approx2.22=OP$.

concepts: Angle of elevation with compass directions (heights and distances)
Inverse cosine and right triangle trigonometry
questions.question: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point $A$ due north of it is $\alpha$ and from a point $B$ at a distance of $9$ units due west of $A$ is $\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\right)$. If the distance of the point $B$ from the tower is $15$ units, then $\cot\alpha$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $A$ is due north and $B$ due west of $A$, so $OA\perp AB$ and $OA^2+AB^2=OB^2$.
solution: Let $O$ be the foot of the tower, $h$ its height, and $\beta=\cos^{-1}\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$ the elevation from $B$; $OB=15$.
$\cos\beta=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$ gives a right triangle with sides $3,2,\sqrt{13}$, so $\tan\beta=\dfrac23$.
$A$ is due north of $O$ and $B$ is due west of $A$, so $\angle OAB=90^\circ$: $OA^2+AB^2=OB^2$, i.e. $OA^2+81=225$ and $OA=12$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\cos\beta$ directly on the slant distance $BP$, avoiding $\tan\beta$.
solution: Now $OA\perp AB$ with $OB=15$, $AB=9$ gives $OA=12$ (a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle scaled by $3$).

useful_results: Compass directions: if $A$ is due north of $O$ and $B$ is due west of $A$, then $OA\perp AB$; $\angle OAB=90^\circ$ and the horizontal distances form a right triangle ($9$-$12$-$15$ here).
$\cot(\text{elevation})=\dfrac{\text{horizontal distance}}{\text{height}}$, so the cotangents from different points are proportional to their distances from the foot.
An angle given as $\cos^{-1}\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$ is read from the right triangle $3,2,\sqrt{13}$: $\sin=\dfrac2{\sqrt{13}}$, $\tan=\dfrac23$.

concepts: Angle of depression from a wall (heights and distances)
Area of a rectangle and the values of $\tan15^\circ$
questions.question: From the top $A$ of a vertical wall $AB$ of height $30$ m, the angles of depression of the top $P$ and bottom $Q$ of a vertical tower $PQ$ are $15^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ respectively, $B$ and $Q$ are on the same horizontal level. If $C$ is a point on $AB$ such that $CB=PQ$, then the area (in m$^2$) of the quadrilateral $BCPQ$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $BCPQ$ is a rectangle with sides $BQ=30\cot60^\circ$ and $PQ=h$; get $h$ from the two depression angles.
solution: Let $PQ=h=CB$ and $BQ=CP=x$, so $BCPQ$ is a rectangle and $AC=30-h$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Sine rule in $\triangle APQ$: its angles are $45^\circ$ at $A$ and $30^\circ$ at $Q$, giving $PQ$ directly.
solution: $\angle PAQ=60^\circ-15^\circ=45^\circ$ (difference of the depressions). At $Q$, $QA$ makes $60^\circ$ with the ground, so $\angle AQP=90^\circ-60^\circ=30^\circ$.
$BQ=30\cot60^\circ=10\sqrt3$, so the area is $(60-20\sqrt3)\cdot10\sqrt3=600\sqrt3-600=600(\sqrt3-1)$. Same answer.

useful_results: Angle of depression from $A$ to a point $=$ angle of elevation of $A$ from that point (alternate angles); the angle subtended at $A$ by $PQ$ is the difference $60^\circ-15^\circ$.
Two vertical segments $CB$ and $PQ$ of equal length with a horizontal join form a rectangle, so the area is (height) $\times$ (horizontal distance).

concepts: Angle of elevation from perpendicular directions (heights and distances)
questions.question: The angle of elevation of the top $P$ of a tower from the feet of one person standing due South of the tower is $45^\circ$ and from the feet of another person standing due west of the tower is $30^\circ$. If the height of the tower is $5$ meters, then distance (in meters) between the two persons is equal to :
questions.key_idea: South and west are perpendicular directions, so the persons and the foot of the tower form a right triangle.
solution: Let the tower be $AB$ with foot $A$ and top $B$ ($AB=5$); let the persons be at $P$ (due south) and $Q$ (due west).
South and west are perpendicular, so $\angle PAQ=90^\circ$.
The slant distances to the top $B$ are $BP=\dfrac{5}{\sin45^\circ}=5\sqrt2$ and $BQ=\dfrac{5}{\sin30^\circ}=10$.

useful_results: For a tower of height $h$, the foot $A$ and two observers at elevations $\theta_1,\theta_2$ along perpendicular directions: $PQ^2=h^2(\cot^2\theta_1+\cot^2\theta_2)$.
Here $25(1+3)=100$. The triangle with legs $5$ and $5\sqrt3$ is a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle, so $PQ$ is twice the short leg.
Slant-edge form: $PQ^2=BP^2+BQ^2-2h^2$ when $\angle PAQ=90^\circ$ (tower $\perp$ ground). Check: $50+100-50=100$.
